summary: This informational document discusses high-level problems and goals for active-active connection at the TRILL edge, extending multipath and fast failover to end stations that connect to a TRILL campus in more than one place.

eli5.summary: If a computer has two cables going to two switches, both should carry traffic. This RFC explains the challenges and goals for making that work with TRILL.

questions: what is active-active connection in trill
what is the trill appointed forwarder problem
subtitle: Why connecting an end station to several TRILL edge switches at once breaks today's mechanisms, and what a fix must achieve.

tldr.problem: End stations with several ports want to use links to several edge TRILL switches at the same time, but the TRILL Appointed Forwarder mechanism cannot support that.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes the target scenario, lists four concrete problems (frame duplication, loopback, address flip-flop and unsynchronized information), and sets requirements and goals for solutions.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational problem statement with no protocol of its own; solutions are left to separate documents.

facts.label: Uplinks to support
facts.value: Two up to at least four

today: RFC 7379 is an Informational problem statement and has not been obsoleted or updated. The Appointed Forwarder mechanism it discusses is defined in RFC 6439.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
TRILL (Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links, RFC 6325) gives loop-free, per-hop multipath forwarding with minimal configuration. It uses IS-IS as its control-plane routing protocol and defines its own header for user data. Inside a TRILL campus, switches can use multiple parallel links, spread load at the flow level, and quickly reconfigure after link or node changes.

Active-active extends the same load spreading and robustness to the connection between end stations and the campus. Such end stations have several ports and attach, directly or through bridges, to several edge TRILL switches (RBridges). Traffic should be spread across those links at flow granularity and recover quickly from topology changes.
sections.eli5: Inside the TRILL network, traffic already uses many roads at once. Active-active means a computer can also use two or more doors into that network at the same time.

sections.title: Terms Used
sections.content: The RFC adds a few terms to those of the RBridge base protocol. A CE is customer equipment, an end station or bridge. MC-LAG (Multi-Chassis Link Aggregation) is a set of proprietary extensions to IEEE 802.1AX-2011 so the aggregated links can end on different switches. A LAALP (Local Active-Active Link Protocol) is any protocol like MC-LAG that runs in a distributed fashion on a CE, its links and the edge RBridges. An edge group is the group of edge RBridges to which at least one CE is multiply attached using a LAALP. A Data Label is a VLAN or a Fine-Grained Label.
sections.eli5: A LAALP is the team rule that lets one computer share several cables, and the edge group is the set of switches on the other end of those cables.

sections.title: The Target Scenario
sections.content:
The existing Appointed Forwarder mechanism (RFC 6439) handles failover, avoids loops, and with configuration can spread load per VLAN. Only one appointed RBridge can ingress or egress native frames for a given VLAN on a link. It relies on edge RBridges exchanging TRILL IS-IS Hello packets through their access ports.

With a LAALP the Hellos from one RBridge are not forwarded to the others by the CE, so each member believes it is the Appointed Forwarder for all VLANs and forwards frames. The mechanism then cannot give active-active or even active-standby service.

Active-active is wanted for flow-based rather than VLAN-based load balancing and for faster failure recovery, since Appointed Forwarder waits for Hello timer expiry, which takes seconds. Today a LAALP is usually proprietary, so edge RBridges often must come from the same vendor.

The RFC assumes the LAALP delivers each frame from an end node to exactly one edge RBridge, never forwards frames between uplinks, tries to keep a flow on one uplink, and accepts frames from any uplink. It also assumes the edge RBridges share a globally unique LAALP ID, learn of each other's failures in a timely fashion, and can exchange information with each other.
sections.eli5: The old way names one switch as the only door for each group of rooms. When a computer has two cables, the switches cannot hear each other, so each one thinks it is in charge and they step on each other's toes.

sections.title: Problems at the TRILL Edge
sections.content:
Four problems must be solved:

  • Frame duplication: when a multi-destination frame enters the campus, every edge group RBridge thinks it is the Appointed Forwarder and sends it to the CE, so the CE gets several copies. This also happens when the ingress is a member of the same edge group. Unicast does not have this problem.
  • Loopback: a multi-destination frame sent by the CE to one member is carried across the campus, and another member decapsulates it and sends it back to the CE.
  • Address flip-flop: if the CE sends frames with the same source MAC address and Data Label through different members, remote RBridges learn that address against different nicknames in turn. Existing hardware overwrites the old attachment, treats this as a severe problem, and may reorder frames.
  • Unsynchronized information: a member that did not learn a remote host's address must flood unknown-unicast return traffic that another member could have avoided.
sections.eli5: Mail can arrive twice, bounce straight back to the sender, make everyone confused about where a computer lives, or make a switch shout to the whole building because it was not told what its neighbor already knew.

sections.title: Requirements and Goals
sections.content:
Solutions are expected to meet these high-level requirements.

Data plane: all uplinks of a CE MUST be active; loopback and frame duplication MUST be prevented; learned Data Label and MAC to nickname mappings MUST NOT flip-flop; packets of a flow SHOULD stay in order; the Reverse Path Forwarding Check MUST still work; and one uplink failure MUST NOT cause persistent delivery failure.

Control plane: no new information is required between edge RBridges and CEs or end nodes. Any TRILL-specific information exchanged within an edge group must have a specified mechanism unless the LAALP handles it, and RBridges SHOULD be able to discover other members of their edge group.

Deployment: minimal configuration, automatic detection of edge group misconfiguration, incremental deployment with changes only on the edge group RBridges, support for two up to at least four active-active uplinks, and no assumption of a dedicated link between edge RBridges.
sections.eli5: A good fix must let every cable work, never send mail twice or back to the sender, keep each computer's address steady, and be easy to set up.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
As an informational overview, the document says it adds no extra security risks. Risks from a particular LAALP or solution are left to the documents that describe them.

End-station links in TRILL are Ethernet links, and the RFC suggests considering link security as described in IEEE Std 802.1AE-2006 to protect end-station data and link-level control messages, including LAALP control messages. General TRILL security is covered in RFC 6325.
sections.eli5: This document only describes problems, so it adds no new dangers. It does suggest locking the cables with link-level security.

items.label: Frame duplications
items.desc: A CE receives several copies of a multi-destination frame.

items.label: Loopback
items.desc: A frame sent by the CE is egressed by another member and returns to it.

items.label: Address flip-flop
items.desc: Remote RBridges keep relearning the MAC address against different nicknames.

items.label: Unsynchronized information
items.desc: Members lack each other's learned mappings and flood unnecessarily.
